Development guide

Introduction

This playbook explains how product and engineering teams use AI to move from uncertain needs to verified software and operational learning. It describes the decisions, evidence and accountability to agree, then shows how Eitri supports the workflow.

The AI-Software Development Lifecycle (AI-SDLC) covers discovery, implementation, release and learning from use. AI-assisted development means work supported by AI tools, whether or not the resulting product contains AI.

Start with your task

Choose the closest task. Each route gives a minimum starting workflow; the accountable owner confirms the applicable controls, evidence and approvals. Add the high-risk route when a feature or defect affects sensitive data, access, public interfaces, major architecture or a hard-to-reverse action.

  • Explore a product ideaState the user problem and a testable assumption → agree a safe experiment and success criteria → test with users → record whether to continue, revise or stop. The product decision owner reviews the evidence before committing to implementation.
  • Deliver a featureAgree scope and acceptance criteria → plan bounded changes → build and verify them → obtain the applicable review and release approvals → monitor the outcome. Keep requirements, test results, unresolved risks and the decision with the change.
  • Fix a defectRecord the observed and expected behaviour → reproduce the failure → assess impact → make a bounded correction and add a regression test → review and release through the applicable controls → verify recovery. If the failure is an active incident, follow the existing incident process first.
  • Make a high-risk changeIdentify affected systems, data and people → involve the relevant security, architecture, data or operational specialists before execution → agree independent checks, recovery and stop conditions → submit evidence and residual risks to the authorised decision-maker. Release only within the agreed authority and monitor the result.

Once the requirements and controls are clear, use the Eitri workflow for tool instructions and the pipeline and pre-production checks for its release support. A short route does not waive an applicable control.

Audience and authority

This guide is for EDS product and engineering teams: product owners and managers, business analysts, designers, developers, technical leads, quality office (QO) and cyber managers, and operational team. Organisational leaders can use it to plan ownership, capability and support.

It combines a proposed organisational playbook with EDS implementation guidance for Eitri, the AI-assisted development workflow described in this site. The playbook explains the reasons and decisions; the implementation pages describe how the current tools support them.

This draft does not establish approved EDS policy or grant approval authority. Confirm the applicable lifecycle, policies and decision owners for your work. Where a control is required, record its authoritative source and the evidence and approval it needs.

Why AI-SDLC?

Product development draws on product management, research, design, engineering, testing, security and operations. When work moves between specialists without timely feedback or enough context, teams can wait longer to discover a mistaken assumption.

In this illustrative sequence, work passes through requirements, design, build, test, approval and launch before user learning returns. Each handoff can introduce waiting or lost context. The dashed path shows the cost of postponing feedback.

Teams using smaller batches and earlier feedback can learn before launch. Specialist capacity, handoffs and the cost of changing direction still matter when introducing AI into those workflows.

AI can help teams draft requirements, build prototypes, write code and run checks with less manual effort. AI-SDLC brings these capabilities into the whole development workflow, with people setting goals, reviewing evidence and deciding what to release. The aim is faster validated learning: testing assumptions early and using the results to decide what to build or change.

  1. Reduce delays between specialists

    Work can stall while a designer waits for clarification, a developer waits for design or a security reviewer waits for architecture. AI can turn shared requirements into draft screens, test cases and questions for security review, giving specialists material to review together earlier.

    Give the AI tool the same requirements, constraints and recorded decisions that the team uses. Product, engineering and security specialists review the drafts, resolve conflicting assumptions and record decisions before dependent work proceeds.

  2. Test assumptions before committing

    Finding that users do not need a solution after months of development can mean substantial rework. AI can help build a small prototype and draft test tasks, reducing the effort needed to put an idea in front of users.

    Choose an assumption that could change the product decision, then test it with users before building the full solution. Use AI to organise the findings, check the summary against the original observations and decide whether to continue, revise or stop.

  3. Explore more options before choosing

    When each alternative takes substantial effort to produce, teams may settle on the first plausible design. AI can draft several interface designs or implementation approaches from the same requirements, making alternatives easier to compare.

    Ask for options with different trade-offs, then test them against the same user needs, constraints and success criteria. Designers and engineers review feasibility and test results before selecting an approach or combining useful parts.

  4. Revise or replace unsuitable code

    Teams can spend more effort patching an unsuitable implementation than trying a different approach. An AI agent is software that uses an AI model and tools to carry out a task. Within agreed permissions, it can help rewrite a small component and run regression tests for comparison.

    Give the agent the required behaviour, interface contracts and tests that the replacement needs to pass. Developers review the changes and test results, then decide whether the replacement improves the solution enough to justify switching.

    Note

    Some decisions remain costly to reverse: core data models, public APIs, regulatory commitments, major architecture choices, vendor dependencies, user migrations and security models. Make these deliberately, with human judgement.

  5. Improve the whole delivery workflow

    AI can produce requirements, code and prototypes faster than the team can review them. If review, testing and user feedback cannot keep pace, work accumulates at the next step and delivery still waits.

    Illustrative examples of how faster tasks can move the bottleneck
    Faster taskIf the rest stays the sameLikely result
    AI drafts more product requestsEngineering capacity is unchangedThe engineering queue can grow
    AI helps developers write code fasterSecurity review capacity is unchangedChanges can queue for security review
    AI helps build prototypes fasterUser testing still takes months to arrangeThe team still waits to learn whether the solution helps

    An agent harness provides instructions, tools and checks for AI to carry out tasks. Use it to connect development work with automated tests, policy checks and review steps.

    Track where work waits, arrange user testing early and improve the slowest step before increasing the volume of generated work.

  6. Check AI outputs as work progresses

    AI can generate code, designs and tests in large volumes, increasing the amount of work that needs checking. An agent harness can run tests and scanners after each change, giving developers feedback while the work is still easy to revise.

    Define the expected behaviour and checks before the agent starts. When a check fails, use the result to correct the work or reconsider the approach.

    Developers review generated tests against the requirements, and relevant specialists assess usability, security and other areas that need judgement. Keep the results with the change so reviewers can see why it is ready to proceed.

  7. Measure time to an informed decision

    AI can increase the number of prototypes, tests and code changes a team produces. Those counts alone do not show whether the team has resolved an important uncertainty or improved an outcome for users.

    Track the time and cost of testing an assumption and reaching a decision. Compare AI-assisted work with the team's previous approach, including the effort spent reviewing, correcting and testing generated outputs.

    Example · discovery: use AI to prototype a clearer upload flow with synthetic documents and simulated recipients. Set an illustrative usability threshold: at least 8 of 10 pilot users submit the intended document unaided. Record wrong-recipient attempts, participant context and preparation, review and testing effort. The product decision owner uses the findings to choose whether to develop a bounded implementation, revise the flow or stop.

    This small pilot provides exploratory usability evidence. Even with no observed wrong-recipient uploads, it cannot establish the absence of rare security failures. Security assurance needs a separate assessment of threats, access boundaries and data handling, with targeted tests and specialist review. Production acceptance also needs the applicable functional, security and operational evidence and authorised release decision.

    Use each decision to choose the next experiment. Check whether AI is helping the team reach useful decisions sooner and whether the resulting changes improve users' experience.

Use and maintain the guide

Return to the guide as your team’s work moves from discovery to delivery and operational learning. Revisit decisions when user behaviour, system behaviour, policy or tool capabilities change.

When you find a gap, record the affected guidance, supporting evidence and the person responsible for resolving it. Confirm changes to operating requirements with the relevant policy or control owner, and keep Eitri instructions aligned with those decisions.

Next step: choose your task route. With the accountable owner, agree the scope, applicable controls, evidence and next decision before using AI to carry out the work.
